publicationTitle: Flood risk exposure of mortgages in England

verifiedTextSamples.extractedText: As part of our work on climate adaption and resilience , we analysed the geographical exposure of regulated mortgage lending to flood risk.

This helps us identify where flooding from rivers, the sea, and surface water could pose the greatest risk, and where we should focus our resources.  We completed analysis for England using flood risk data from the Environment Agency.

We also completed analysis for the risks across Scotland and Wales; however, the differences in geography and population density meant that we could not apply the methodology consistently across all countries.
Northern Ireland does not have similar flood risk data available.
Since 2005, firms have been required to report data on all new sales of regulated mortgage contracts.
Since 1 April 2021, reporting has also included internal product transfers and further advances completed on or after that date.
This data helps us understand the approximate location of mortgage lending.
We mapped mortgage postcode locations against Environment Agency flood risk datasets covering rivers, the sea and surface water.
The analysis uses postcode-level flood risk classifications rather than individual property data.
It should therefore be viewed as an indicator of overall exposure, not property-specific risk.  Flood risk is classified into bands that reflect the likelihood of flooding.
For rivers and the sea, the bands are very low, low, medium and high (see note 1 ).
For surface water, the bands are low, medium and high.  A postcode is assigned to a risk band when its centroid, the approximate centre of the postcode, falls within a flood risk area.

1. England: Environment Agency Risk of Flooding from Rivers and the Sea: High - greater than or equal to 3.3% chance in any given year (1 in 30)  Medium - less than 3.3% (1 in 30) but greater than or equal to 1% (1 in 100) chance in any given year  Low - less than 1% (1 in 100) but greater than or equal to 0.1% (1 in 1,000) chance in any given year  Very Low - less than 0.1% chance in any given year (1 in 1,000) Risk of Flooding from Surface Water: High - greater than or equal to 3.3% (1 in 30) chance in any given year Medium - less than 3.3% (1 in 30) but greater than or equal to 1% (1 in 100) chance in any given year Low - less than 1% (1 in 100) but greater than or equal to 0.1% (1 in 1,000) chance in any given year.
Our analysis suggests that 15.5% of mortgage contracts in England are linked to postcodes with some level of flood risk.

Exposure varies by region and type of flooding.  These findings help identify where physical climate risks may be most relevant to mortgage lending and where consumers could be more exposed to the impacts of flooding over time.

High-risk exposure to surface water flooding is concentrated in and around London, with Essex showing the highest proportion of postcode centroids in the high-risk category (6.5%).  Exposure to flooding from rivers and the sea is highest in Lincolnshire and East Yorkshire, where a large portion of postcodes fall within the medium and high-risk categories.  Understanding these geographical patterns helps identify where climate-related risks may have the greatest effect on consumers and mortgage lending if flooding becomes more frequent or severe.
Sub-regions from the International Territorial Level (ITL2) are used to provide consistently sized geographical areas across the country.
They are part of the official geographic boundary standards used to break down the country into regions for collecting, publishing and comparing official statistics.
Tables have been ordered by the sum of the medium and high-risk categories.

We analysed mortgage contracts sold in the last reporting period to assess whether lending patterns differ across areas with different levels of flood risk.  In the charts below, each group of bars should be viewed separately.
The percentages show the proportion of mortgages within each LTV band that are linked to postcodes in each flood risk category.
For example, of mortgage contracts with an LTV ratio of 0-10%, around 6% are linked to postcodes classified as low risk for surface water flooding.
For the risk of flooding from surface water, the proportion of mortgages in high-risk areas falls slightly as the LTV ratios increase.
Overall, the proportions remain relatively stable, although there is a notable increase in mortgages with an LTV in excess of 100% in medium-risk areas.
Overall, the results do not show a clear or consistent relationship between higher LTV lending and greater exposure to flood risk.  Chart Data table Download Chart Data table Download
We also analysed flood risk exposure across different levels of deprivation.  The IMD is the official measure of deprivation in England.

It combines information on income, employment, education and skills, health, crime, barriers to housing and services, and the living environment.  The charts below show how flood risk exposure varies across these measures.

Looking at the combined proportion of the red and orange bands helps identify where more deprived communities may be exposed to flood risk.  Chart Data table Download Chart Data table Download Exposure to surface water flooding is broadly similar across deprivation levels.
Within each flood risk band, a higher proportion of mortgages are linked to postcodes in the most deprived areas than to postcodes with no flood risk.
For flooding from rivers and the sea, exposure is spread across all deprivation levels.
As flood risk increases, a larger proportion of mortgages are linked to less deprived areas.

This may reflect the attractiveness of some properties located near rivers or along the coast.  These findings suggest that physical climate risks can affect a wide range of consumers and communities.
They also show that the relationship between flood risk and deprivation can vary depending on the type of flooding.
This analysis provides an overview of the exposure of mortgage lending to flood risk in England.

We found that around 1 in 7 mortgage contracts are linked to postcodes with some level of flood risk, although exposure varies by region and type of flooding.  The findings show that physical climate risks are relevant to mortgage markets because they affect consumers, firms, and market functioning.

However, the results should not be interpreted as an assessment of individual properties, firms or consumer outcomes.  Instead, the analysis is a high-level view of exposure using publicly available flood risk data and mortgage postcode information.
It supports our wider work to improve understanding of how climate-related risks may affect financial services and the challenges of climate adaption and resilience.
This analysis estimates mortgage exposure using postcode centroids rather than individual property locations.

We found that around 1 in 7 mortgage contracts are linked to postcodes with some level of flood risk, although exposure varies by region and type of flooding. The findings show that physical climate risks are relevant to mortgage markets because they affect consumers, firms, and market functioning. Instead, the analysis is a high-level view of exposure using publicly available flood risk data and mortgage postcode information. It supports our wider work to improve understanding of how climate-related risks may affect financial services and the challenges of climate adaption and resilience. This means some properties may be assigned to a different flood risk category than their actual location, particularly in larger rural postcodes or postcodes that cross flood risk boundaries. This approach also cannot capture variation within a postcode. For example, a property may have a lower flood risk than the postcode centroid if it is on higher ground away from a river or flood-prone area. Results are also sensitive to the location of flood risk boundaries. Small differences in location can lead to different risk categorisations, even where actual levels of risk are similar. Postcode centroids are likely to provide more accurate representation in smaller, densely populated postcodes than in larger postcodes with more spread-out properties. Flood risks that are concentrated in small areas are likely to also be underrepresented. Our methodology estimates the probability of flooding at postcode level rather than for individual properties. The results should therefore be viewed as indicators of exposure, not property-level risk assessments. The analysis is intended to support understanding of aggregated exposure and regional pattern identification, but nothing more granular. This analysis does not introduce new regulatory requirements or supervisory expectations. askRiEvidence.normalisedArticleHtml:
Climate-related risks are increasingly relevant to financial services, affecting consumer outcomes and the effective functioning of markets. We examine how flood risk relates to the mortgage market in England and how it may impact different communities.

1. Introduction

As part of our work on climate adaption and resilience, we analysed the geographical exposure of regulated mortgage lending to flood risk. This helps us identify where flooding from rivers, the sea, and surface water could pose the greatest risk, and where we should focus our resources. 

We completed analysis for England using flood risk data from the Environment Agency. We also completed analysis for the risks across Scotland and Wales; however, the differences in geography and population density meant that we could not apply the methodology consistently across all countries. Northern Ireland does not have similar flood risk data available.

Since 2005, firms have been required to report data on all new sales of regulated mortgage contracts. Since 1 April 2021, reporting has also included internal product transfers and further advances completed on or after that date. This data helps us understand the approximate location of mortgage lending.

We mapped mortgage postcode locations against Environment Agency flood risk datasets covering rivers, the sea and surface water. The analysis uses postcode-level flood risk classifications rather than individual property data. It should therefore be viewed as an indicator of overall exposure, not property-specific risk. 

Flood risk is classified into bands that reflect the likelihood of flooding. For rivers and the sea, the bands are very low, low, medium and high (see note 1). For surface water, the bands are low, medium and high.  A postcode is assigned to a risk band when its centroid, the approximate centre of the postcode, falls within a flood risk area.  

Note 1

1. England: Environment Agency

Risk of Flooding from Rivers and the Sea:

High - greater than or equal to 3.3% chance in any given year (1 in 30) 
Medium - less than 3.3% (1 in 30) but greater than or equal to 1% (1 in 100) chance in any given year 
Low - less than 1% (1 in 100) but greater than or equal to 0.1% (1 in 1,000) chance in any given year 
Very Low - less than 0.1% chance in any given year (1 in 1,000)

Risk of Flooding from Surface Water:

High - greater than or equal to 3.3% (1 in 30) chance in any given year

Medium - less than 3.3% (1 in 30) but greater than or equal to 1% (1 in 100) chance in any given year

Low - less than 1% (1 in 100) but greater than or equal to 0.1% (1 in 1,000) chance in any given year.

2. Overview

Our analysis suggests that 15.5% of mortgage contracts in England are linked to postcodes with some level of flood risk. Exposure varies by region and type of flooding. 

These findings help identify where physical climate risks may be most relevant to mortgage lending and where consumers could be more exposed to the impacts of flooding over time.

Flood risk exposure is not evenly distributed across England (see notes 2 and 3). High-risk exposure to surface water flooding is concentrated in and around London, with Essex showing the highest proportion of postcode centroids in the high-risk category (6.5%). 

Exposure to flooding from rivers and the sea is highest in Lincolnshire and East Yorkshire, where a large portion of postcodes fall within the medium and high-risk categories. 

Understanding these geographical patterns helps identify where climate-related risks may have the greatest effect on consumers and mortgage lending if flooding becomes more frequent or severe.

4. High loan-to-value (LTV) ratios

We analysed mortgage contracts sold in the last reporting period to assess whether lending patterns differ across areas with different levels of flood risk. 

In the charts below, each group of bars should be viewed separately. The percentages show the proportion of mortgages within each LTV band that are linked to postcodes in each flood risk category. For example, of mortgage contracts with an LTV ratio of 0-10%, around 6% are linked to postcodes classified as low risk for surface water flooding.

For the risk of flooding from surface water, the proportion of mortgages in high-risk areas falls slightly as the LTV ratios increase. Overall, the proportions remain relatively stable, although there is a notable increase in mortgages with an LTV in excess of 100% in medium-risk areas.

Overall, the results do not show a clear or consistent relationship between higher LTV lending and greater exposure to flood risk.

5. Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD)

We also analysed flood risk exposure across different levels of deprivation. 

The IMD is the official measure of deprivation in England. It combines information on income, employment, education and skills, health, crime, barriers to housing and services, and the living environment. 

The charts below show how flood risk exposure varies across these measures. Looking at the combined proportion of the red and orange bands helps identify where more deprived communities may be exposed to flood risk.

Exposure to surface water flooding is broadly similar across deprivation levels. Within each flood risk band, a higher proportion of mortgages are linked to postcodes in the most deprived areas than to postcodes with no flood risk.

For flooding from rivers and the sea, exposure is spread across all deprivation levels. As flood risk increases, a larger proportion of mortgages are linked to less deprived areas. This may reflect the attractiveness of some properties located near rivers or along the coast. 

These findings suggest that physical climate risks can affect a wide range of consumers and communities. They also show that the relationship between flood risk and deprivation can vary depending on the type of flooding.

6. Conclusions

This analysis provides an overview of the exposure of mortgage lending to flood risk in England. We found that around 1 in 7 mortgage contracts are linked to postcodes with some level of flood risk, although exposure varies by region and type of flooding. 

The findings show that physical climate risks are relevant to mortgage markets because they affect consumers, firms, and market functioning. However, the results should not be interpreted as an assessment of individual properties, firms or consumer outcomes. 

Instead, the analysis is a high-level view of exposure using publicly available flood risk data and mortgage postcode information. It supports our wider work to improve understanding of how climate-related risks may affect financial services and the challenges of climate adaption and resilience.

Caveats and limitations

This analysis estimates mortgage exposure using postcode centroids rather than individual property locations. This means some properties may be assigned to a different flood risk category than their actual location, particularly in larger rural postcodes or postcodes that cross flood risk boundaries. 

This approach also cannot capture variation within a postcode. For example, a property may have a lower flood risk than the postcode centroid if it is on higher ground away from a river or flood-prone area. 

Results are also sensitive to the location of flood risk boundaries. Small differences in location can lead to different risk categorisations, even where actual levels of risk are similar. Postcode centroids are likely to provide more accurate representation in smaller, densely populated postcodes than in larger postcodes with more spread-out properties. Flood risks that are concentrated in small areas are likely to also be underrepresented.

Our methodology estimates the probability of flooding at postcode level rather than for individual properties. The results should therefore be viewed as indicators of exposure, not property-level risk assessments. 

The analysis is intended to support understanding of aggregated exposure and regional pattern identification, but nothing more granular. This analysis does not introduce new regulatory requirements or supervisory expectations.

evidenceBlocks.extractedText: As part of our work on climate adaption and resilience , we analysed the geographical exposure of regulated mortgage lending to flood risk.

This helps us identify where flooding from rivers, the sea, and surface water could pose the greatest risk, and where we should focus our resources.  We completed analysis for England using flood risk data from the Environment Agency.

We also completed analysis for the risks across Scotland and Wales; however, the differences in geography and population density meant that we could not apply the methodology consistently across all countries.
Northern Ireland does not have similar flood risk data available.
Since 2005, firms have been required to report data on all new sales of regulated mortgage contracts.
Since 1 April 2021, reporting has also included internal product transfers and further advances completed on or after that date.
This data helps us understand the approximate location of mortgage lending.
We mapped mortgage postcode locations against Environment Agency flood risk datasets covering rivers, the sea and surface water.
The analysis uses postcode-level flood risk classifications rather than individual property data.
It should therefore be viewed as an indicator of overall exposure, not property-specific risk.  Flood risk is classified into bands that reflect the likelihood of flooding.
For rivers and the sea, the bands are very low, low, medium and high (see note 1 ).
For surface water, the bands are low, medium and high.  A postcode is assigned to a risk band when its centroid, the approximate centre of the postcode, falls within a flood risk area.

1. England: Environment Agency Risk of Flooding from Rivers and the Sea: High - greater than or equal to 3.3% chance in any given year (1 in 30)  Medium - less than 3.3% (1 in 30) but greater than or equal to 1% (1 in 100) chance in any given year  Low - less than 1% (1 in 100) but greater than or equal to 0.1% (1 in 1,000) chance in any given year  Very Low - less than 0.1% chance in any given year (1 in 1,000) Risk of Flooding from Surface Water: High - greater than or equal to 3.3% (1 in 30) chance in any given year Medium - less than 3.3% (1 in 30) but greater than or equal to 1% (1 in 100) chance in any given year Low - less than 1% (1 in 100) but greater than or equal to 0.1% (1 in 1,000) chance in any given year.
Our analysis suggests that 15.5% of mortgage contracts in England are linked to postcodes with some level of flood risk.

Exposure varies by region and type of flooding.  These findings help identify where physical climate risks may be most relevant to mortgage lending and where consumers could be more exposed to the impacts of flooding over time.
